title: Transformations
intro: If X has a known distribution, so does g(X). For monotone maps there is a formula; for any distribution there is a way to generate it from a uniform random number.

blocks.text: The general approach is to compute the CDF of $Y = g(X)$ directly: $F_Y(y) = P(g(X)\le y)$, rewrite the event in terms of $X$, and differentiate if a density is wanted. For $Y = X^2$ with $X$ uniform on $(0, 1)$: $P(Y\le y) = P(X\le\sqrt y) = \sqrt y$, so $f_Y(y) = 1/(2\sqrt y)$, a density that is infinite at 0 yet integrates to 1.

blocks.caption: For a strictly monotone, differentiable g.

blocks.text: The derivative factor accounts for stretching: where $g$ spreads an interval out, the density thins. For several variables the same formula holds with the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant of the inverse map; that is how the Box–Muller transform below is derived. Linear maps are the simplest case: if $Y = aX + b$ then $f_Y(y) = f_X((y - b)/a)/\vert a\vert$.

If $U$ is uniform on $(0, 1)$ and $F$ is any CDF, then $X = F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$, because $P(F^{-1}(U)\le x) = P(U\le F(x)) = F(x)$. Conversely, $F(X)$ is uniform when $F$ is continuous (the probability integral transform). Every random number generator for a named distribution is ultimately built on uniform random numbers, by this or by a cleverer route such as Box–Muller or rejection sampling (Monte Carlo Methods (#/probability/limit-theorems/monte-carlo)).

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
u = rng.random(10 ** 6)
# Inverse-transform sampling: F^{-1}(U) has CDF F. For Exp(2), F^{-1}(u) = -ln(1-u)/2
x = -np.log(1 - u) / 2
print(f"-ln(1-U)/2: mean {x.mean():.4f} (1/2), P(X > 1) = {np.mean(x > 1):.4f} (e^-2 = {np.exp(-2):.4f})")
# Change of variables: if X ~ Uniform(0,1), Y = X^2 has density 1/(2 sqrt y) on (0,1)
y = u ** 2
for a, b in ((0, 0.01), (0.25, 0.36), (0.81, 1.0)):
    print(f"P({a} < X^2 < {b}): simulated {np.mean((y > a) & (y < b)):.4f}, from the density {np.sqrt(b) - np.sqrt(a):.4f}")
# Box-Muller: two uniforms -> two independent standard normals
u1, u2 = rng.random(500000), rng.random(500000)
r = np.sqrt(-2 * np.log(u1)); z1, z2 = r * np.cos(2 * np.pi * u2), r * np.sin(2 * np.pi * u2)
print(f"Box-Muller: means {z1.mean():+.4f} {z2.mean():+.4f}, variances {z1.var():.4f} {z2.var():.4f}, correlation {np.corrcoef(z1, z2)[0, 1]:+.4f}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: $-\ln(1 - U)/2$ has mean 0.4999 and $P(X > 1) = 0.1354$, matching Exp(2) ($1/2$ and $e^{-2} = 0.1353$). For $Y = U^2$, the three intervals each have probability 0.100 by simulation and from the density. Box–Muller produces two normal samples with means near 0, variances near 1 and correlation $+0.003$.

blocks.title: Square root of an exponential
blocks.text: $X\sim$ Exp(1) and $Y = \sqrt X$. Find the density of $Y$.

blocks.title: Sampling a Pareto
blocks.text: Give a formula that turns a uniform $U$ into a sample with CDF $F(x) = 1 - x^{-\alpha}$ for $x\ge1$.
solution: Since $1 - U$ is also uniform, $U^{-1/\alpha}$ works too.

blocks.title: A log-normal
blocks.text: If $X\sim N(0, 1)$, what is the median of $Y = e^X$, and is it the mean?
solution: $e^x$ is increasing, so the median of $Y$ is $e^{\text{median}(X)} = e^0 = 1$.
The mean is $E[e^X] = e^{1/2}\approx1.65$ (from the normal MGF). Medians pass through monotone maps; means do not.
